title: The Internet Doesn't Know How to Be CEO
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell argues that the internet gave CEOs a flood of contradictory advice and that generic AI now merely synthesizes it into polished, balanced maxims that all collapse into the phrase it depends. Using the question of how closely a CEO should listen to customers, he shows that both listen to customers and customers do not know what they want are endlessly cited and both have produced successful companies. He warns that an averaged answer keeps a company average and that a chatbot tends to mirror the framing of whoever asks, which amounts to confirmation bias with better bullet points. His remedy is to give AI two things it lacks: a system for the CEO job that weighs customers, employees, and shareholders together, and secure operating context about the company's strategy, market, and economics. With both in place, the AI can ask what a decision depends on rather than stopping at it depends. The piece closes by noting that the real prize is advice matched to the company in front of you.
points: Generic AI turns a thousand contradictory pieces of business advice into a respectable middle that always ends in it depends, which is exactly the point where a CEO is supposed to decide.
Averaging opposing advice is a reliable way to remain an average company, so balance is not the same as good judgment.
Because chatbots mirror the framing of the question, an anxious CEO is nudged to listen more to customers and a confident one is nudged to ignore them, producing confirmation bias on steroids.
A CEO decision always moves a triangle of customers, employees, and shareholders, so a useful AI needs a system that shows what a choice does to all three corners.
With secure knowledge of the company's strategy, market maturity, and finances, AI can shift from it depends to what it depends on, which is where it becomes genuinely helpful.
quotes: The Internet gave us a thousand contradictory answers. AI can now read all thousand, reconcile the contradictions, sand off the sharp edges, and hand us a polished synthesis. It is masterful at caveats.
Of course it depends! The whole reason the CEO exists is because they look at “It depends” and say “We’re doing this, and here’s why.
Taking the average of opposing advice does not produce a good decision. In fact, taking averages is a pretty reliable way to keep a company average.
If AI is simply reflecting your framing back at you, more fluently and with better bullet points, you have confirmation bias on steroids.
The CEO operates at the intersection of three constituencies: customers, employees, and shareholders. Pushing hard toward one corner of that triangle means the force moves through the other two.
Now it can move beyond “it depends.” It can begin asking: What does it depend on?
The real prize is an AI that knows enough about the CEO’s job and the company in front of it to know which advice matters now.
